blocks.content: A bicameral legislature ensures thorough scrutiny of legislation and prevents hasty lawmaking through dual parliamentary deliberation.

rows: Single Legislative Body (Vidhan Sabha / Lower House)
Slower lawmaking due to dual scrutiny, higher expenditure
Direct representation; risk of dominant hasty lawmaking
Provides double check on legislation and represents varied interests/states
Adopted by 22 Indian States and UTs with assemblies
Adopted at the Center (Parliament) and in 6 Indian States

items: Remember the six bicameral states using the acronym KUMBAT: Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
Article 169 permits creation or abolition of Vidhan Parishad by Parliament via a Simple Majority, following a Special Majority resolution passed by the state Vidhan Sabha.
The Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) is a permanent house that cannot be dissolved; members serve 6-year terms with one-third retiring every two years.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: A unicameral legislature consists of a single legislative chamber, whereas a bicameral legislature comprises two separate houses: the Upper House and the Lower House.
At the Union level, India features a bicameral Parliament comprising the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
As per Article 168 of the Constitution, state legislatures in India may be either unicameral or bicameral.
Currently, six Indian states possess bicameral legislatures: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
Under Article 169, Parliament can create or abolish a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) if the state's Legislative Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority.
